questions.text: Which one of the following regular expressions is equivalent to the language accepted by the DFA given below?
questions.solution:
The start state loops on 0 and goes to the final state on 1; the final state loops on 0 and returns on 1. So the DFA accepts strings with an odd number of 1s.

[latex]0^*1(0+10^*1)^*[/latex]: [latex]0^*[/latex] stays at start, [latex]1[/latex] reaches the final state, then [latex]0[/latex] (self-loop) or [latex]10^*1[/latex] (go back and return) keeps it final. This is exactly "odd number of 1s".

Others fail on "1" (odd, accepted): [latex]0^*(10^*11)^*0^*[/latex], [latex]0^*1(010^*1)^*0^*[/latex] cannot give "111", and [latex]0(1+0^*10^*1)^*0^*[/latex] must start with 0.

Answer: [latex]0^*1(0+10^*1)^*[/latex]

questions.text:
Consider the following two regular expressions over the alphabet [latex] \{0,1\} [/latex] :

[latex] \begin{aligned} & r=0^*+1^* \\ & s=01^*+10^* \end{aligned} [/latex]

The total number of strings of length less than or equal to 5 , which are neither in [latex] r [/latex] nor in [latex] s [/latex], is ____
questions.solution:
Total strings of length 0 to 5: [latex]1+2+4+8+16+32=63[/latex].

- [latex]r=0^*+1^*[/latex]: [latex]\epsilon[/latex], plus all-0 and all-1 strings of each length 1-5: [latex]1+2\times5=11[/latex].
- [latex]s=01^*+10^*[/latex]: for each length 1-5, the strings [latex]01\ldots1[/latex] and [latex]10\ldots0[/latex]. Length 1 ("0", "1") is already in r, so new ones = [latex]2\times4=8[/latex].

In r or s: [latex]11+8=19[/latex]. Neither: [latex]63-19=44[/latex].

Answer: 44

questions.text: Let [latex] G=(V, \Sigma, S, P) [/latex] be a context-free grammar in Chomsky Normal Form with [latex] \Sigma=\{a, b, c\} [/latex] and [latex] V [/latex] containing 10 variable symbols including the start symbol [latex] S [/latex]. The string [latex] w=a^{30} b^{30} c^{30} [/latex] is derivable from [latex] S [/latex]. The number of steps (application of rules) in the derivation [latex] S \rightarrow^* w [/latex] is _____
questions.solution:
CNF rules are [latex]A\rightarrow BC[/latex] or [latex]A\rightarrow a[/latex].

- Each [latex]A\rightarrow BC[/latex] increases the number of symbols by 1. To grow from 1 symbol (S) to [latex]n[/latex] symbols needs [latex]n-1[/latex] such steps.
- Each of the [latex]n[/latex] variables is then turned into a terminal by [latex]A\rightarrow a[/latex]: [latex]n[/latex] steps.

Total [latex]=2n-1[/latex]. Here [latex]n=|w|=90[/latex]: [latex]2(90)-1=179[/latex].

Answer: 179

questions.text:
Consider the 5 -state DFA [latex] M [/latex] accepting the language [latex] L(M) \subset(0+1)^* [/latex] shown below. For any string [latex] w \in(0+1)^* [/latex] let [latex] n_0(w) [/latex] be the number of [latex] 0^{\prime} s [/latex] in [latex] w [/latex] and [latex] n_1(w) [/latex] be the number of 1 's in [latex] w [/latex].

Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
questions.solution:
Reading 0 moves 1[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]2[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]3[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]1, reading 1 moves 1[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]4[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]5[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]1, and the reverse arrows undo a step. So the DFA tracks [latex](n_0-n_1)\bmod 3[/latex]:
state 1 = 0, states 2 and 5 = 1, states 3 and 4 = 2.

[latex]L(M)=\{w: n_0(w)\equiv n_1(w)\pmod 3\}[/latex], and states with the same value are equivalent.

- 2 and 4 (values 1 and 2): distinguishable (input "1": 2[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]1 accept, 4[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]5 reject) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- 3 and 4: both value 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] equivalent [latex]\text{---}[/latex] statement FALSE.
- 2 and 5: both value 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] equivalent [latex]\text{---}[/latex] statement FALSE.
- [latex]n_0=n_1[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] difference 0 [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] accepted [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: "States 3 and 4 are distinguishable" and "States 2 and 5 are distinguishable"

questions.text: Let [latex]L_1, L_2 [/latex] be two regular languages and [latex]L_3 [/latex] a language which is not regular. Which of the following statements is/are always TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]L_1\cap\overline{L_2}=\phi[/latex] only means [latex]L_1\subseteq L_2[/latex]. Equality also needs [latex]L_2\subseteq L_1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]L_1\cup L_3[/latex] can be regular: take [latex]L_1=\Sigma^*[/latex], then [latex]L_1\cup L_3=\Sigma^*[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE (not always).
- If [latex]\overline{L_3}[/latex] were regular, then its complement [latex]L_3[/latex] would be regular (closure under complement). So [latex]\overline{L_3}[/latex] is not regular [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Regular languages are closed under complement and union, so [latex]\overline{L_1}\cup\overline{L_2}[/latex] is regular [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: [latex]\overline{L_3}[/latex] is not regular; [latex]\overline{L_1}\cup\overline{L_2}[/latex] is regular
